narrative.text: A statement arrives from Armadine Industries. The private placement you invested in at the beginning of your Chancellorship has matured. The company's share price has risen substantially — government infrastructure contracts and military procurement have been good for business. Your original investment of 3,000 ₭ is now worth 8,000 ₭. The statement is accompanied by a letter from Mikhael Dorin, whose tone suggests he believes he has established a mutually beneficial relationship that will continue.

The return is substantial — more than double what I put in. Every infrastructure project I approved, every military contract I signed, every budget allocation that benefited the steel industry — those were policy decisions made in what I believed was the national interest. But they also benefited Armadine, and by extension, they benefited me. That is the problem. Not that I made bad decisions — that even good decisions now look compromised. If steel was nationalized, the situation is different: the investment is worthless, and my decision to nationalize — however justified — just cost my family 3,000 ₭. Either way, the entanglement I accepted has consequences. The question is whether I accept them gracefully.

choices.text: "Accept the return. The 8,000 ₭ is the legitimate outcome of a legal investment. I invested in a Veltrian industrial company because I believed in Veltrian industry — and that belief has been vindicated. My policy decisions were made in the national interest, not in my financial interest. If critics want to draw a line between the two, let them — but they will be drawing a false equivalence. I did not trade on inside information. I did not sell policy decisions. I invested in my country, and my country's economy grew. That is what investments are supposed to do. Transfer the funds to my account."

"The investment is gone. When Vael's industrial holdings were nationalized, Armadine's share value collapsed, and the private placement was wiped out. There is nothing to collect — only the knowledge that I made a policy decision that cost my family 3,000 ₭, and that I would make it again. The nationalization was the right decision for the country. Losing this investment was the price of making it. I will not complain about paying it."

"The investment is gone — absorbed by the war economy. When strategic industries were nationalized for the war effort, Armadine was included. Private shareholders, including those in the pre-listing placement, were not compensated. The 3,000 ₭ is lost. There is no recourse. In the context of what the country is facing, a lost investment is the least of anyone's concerns — including mine. The country needed steel for the war. My portfolio does not matter. It never did."
